content: Sodium thiosulfate (Na2S2O3) is a colorless crystalline compound, most commonly encountered as its pentahydrate form, Na2S2O3·5H2O. This pentahydrate is an efflorescent, monoclinic crystalline substance, also referred to as sodium hyposulfite or hypo. The thiosulfate anion (S2O3^2−) has a tetrahedral structure and is conceptually derived from a sulfate anion by replacing one oxygen atom with a sulfur atom. The bond length between the two sulfur atoms suggests a single bond, indicating that the terminal sulfur atom carries a significant negative charge, while the sulfur-oxygen bonds exhibit partial double-bond character. The first protonation of the thiosulfate anion occurs at the sulfur atom. On an industrial scale, sodium thiosulfate is primarily produced as a byproduct from the liquid waste of sodium sulfide or sulfur dye manufacturing processes. In laboratory settings, it can be synthesized by boiling an aqueous solution of sodium sulfite with sulfur. The S2O3^2− anion serves as a water-soluble form of elemental sulfur. The thiosulfate anion reacts with dilute acids to produce sulfur, sulfur dioxide, and water. This reaction is utilized to generate colloidal sulfur. When protonation occurs at low temperatures, thiosulfuric acid (H2S2O3) can be isolated. Thiosulfuric acid is a strong acid with pKa values of 0.6 and 1.7. In analytical chemistry, sodium thiosulfate is widely used in iodometry due to its ability to react stoichiometrically with iodine. In this reaction, thiosulfate reduces iodine to iodide while being oxidized to tetrathionate. This quantitative reaction, combined with the excellent shelf-life of sodium thiosulfate pentahydrate, makes it a reliable titrant in iodometric analyses. It is also employed in iodine clock experiments and in determining the oxygen content of water through a series of reactions. In photographic processing, sodium thiosulfate is known as a photographic fixer. It dissolves silver halides, such as silver bromide (AgBr), which are components of photographic emulsions. This application, discovered by John Herschel, is used in both film and paper processing. Sodium thiosulfate is also used as an alternative lixiviant to cyanide in gold extraction. It forms a strong complex with gold(I) ions, making it suitable for leaching gold from ores that are refractory to cyanidation, such as carbonaceous or Carlin-type ores. The advantages of this method include the non-toxic nature of thiosulfate. However, challenges include high thiosulfate consumption and the lack of an effective recovery technique, as the gold-thiosulfate complex does not adsorb onto activated carbon, which is the standard method in cyanidation. Other applications of sodium thiosulfate include: Serving as a component in hand warmers and chemical heating pads, where it produces heat through exothermic crystallization of a supercooled solution. Neutralizing bleach to allow pH testing with liquid indicators, as bleach destroys most pH indicators. Dechlorinating tap water for aquariums or treating wastewater effluent before release into rivers. This process requires 0.1–0.3 grams of sodium thiosulfate pentahydrate per 10 liters of water. Reducing chlorine levels in swimming pools and spas after superchlorination. Removing iodine stains, such as those caused by nitrogen triiodide explosions. Acting as an antidote for cyanide poisoning by donating sulfur for the enzymatic conversion of cyanide to thiocyanate, which is excreted in urine. Being used in bacteriological water assessments. Playing a role in the tanning of leather. Demonstrating reaction rates in chemistry classes, as the thiosulfate ion decomposes into sulfite and colloidal sulfur in an acid-catalyzed reaction. Demonstrating supercooling in physics classes, as melted sodium thiosulfate can be supercooled to room temperature and crystallization releases heat, raising the temperature to 48.3°C. Being included in patina recipes for copper alloys. Acting as an anionic surfactant in pharmaceutical preparations to aid in dispersion. Treating calciphylaxis in hemodialysis patients with end-stage renal disease.
